# Library Ambiguity

This example shows how a Java application can compile successfully and still run
with the wrong library implementation at runtime.

The problem is not that Maven cannot resolve dependencies. The problem is that
the runtime classpath can still contain more than one version of the same
library. Once that happens, the JVM loads the first matching class it finds, and
the application behavior becomes a function of classpath contents and ordering
rather than your intended dependency version.

That matters for secure coding because library ambiguity can silently
reintroduce buggy or vulnerable code even after you think you have upgraded to a
safer version.

The trust boundary is the packaged runtime layout: build and deployment tooling
can place JARs there that the application does not control at class-load time.
The unsafe default is a wildcard classpath containing duplicate classes. Its
failure mode is that an older, vulnerable implementation can win class loading
without any source-code or Maven dependency change. This exercise compares that
default with explicit runtime packaging and classpath control.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this example, attendees can:

- identify how two versions of the same library enter one runtime layout;
- trace the difference between Maven dependency mediation and JVM class loading;
- demonstrate that wildcard classpath ordering changes the implementation used
  at runtime; and
- explain how explicit dependency management and controlled runtime packaging
  reduce, but do not eliminate, supply-chain risk.

## Prerequisites

- [Oracle Java 25 or newer](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/#java25)

## The program to inspect

Before running anything, inspect what the example is modelling.

There are two versions of library `A`. Both define the same class,
`demo_a.LibA`, but they return different messages. The older version represents
the buggy implementation; the newer version represents the fixed one.

- The older version

  ```java
  package demo_a;

  public final class LibA {
      public String hello() {
          return "¡Hola Mundo! This version has a bug!";
      }
  }
  ```

- The newer version

  ```java
  package demo_a;

  public final class LibA {
      public String hello() {
          return "Hello, World! Bug free, as you can see.";
      }
  }
  ```

The application depends directly on `A` version `1.1.0`, but it also depends on
library `B`, and `B` itself depends on `A` version `1.0.0`.

```xml
<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>demo</groupId>
        <artifactId>B</artifactId>
        <version>1.0.0</version>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>demo</groupId>
        <artifactId>A</artifactId>
        <version>1.1.0</version>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>
```

The application depends directly on `A` version `1.1.0`, but it also depends on
library `B`, and `B` itself depends on `A` version `1.0.0`.

```xml
<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>demo</groupId>
        <artifactId>A</artifactId>
        <version>1.0.0</version>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>
```

Finally, look at the application entry point. It calls `LibA` in two ways:

- indirectly through `LibB`
- directly from the application

This is important because both calls will end up using whichever `demo_a.LibA` class the JVM
loads first at runtime.

```java
package demo;

import demo_a.LibA;
import demo_b.LibB;

public final class Main {
    public static void main(final String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Hello");
        System.out.println("LibB: " + new LibB().sayHello());
        System.out.println("LibA: " + new LibA().hello());
    }
}
```

## Guided walkthrough

Run these commands from this example directory. They create only the local
`target/` build output; they do not change system configuration or download an
unreviewed runtime dependency outside Maven’s normal build process.

1. Build the full Maven reactor.

  A successful build creates a reproducible runtime layout containing both
  versions of library `A` and copy all JAR files to the `target/libs`
  directory.

   ```shell
   ./mvnw clean package
   ```

2. Inspect the generated runtime layout.

   This confirms that both versions of library `A` are available side by side at
   runtime.

   ```shell
   tree --dirsfirst --sort=name 'target/libs'
   ```

   Generated runtime libraries

   ```
   target/libs
   ├── A-1.0.0.jar
   ├── A-1.1.0.jar
   ├── app-1.0.0.jar
   └── B-1.0.0.jar

   1 directory, 4 files
   ```

   The important observation is that there is no longer a single unambiguous
   `A` JAR on disk. At this point the runtime classpath can easily drift away
   from the version Maven selected during dependency mediation.

3. Ask Maven for the dependency tree of the `app` module.

   This shows Maven’s compile-time view. It resolves the direct dependency on
   `A` version `1.1.0` for the application, so the dependency tree looks clean
   even though both versions remain available in the runtime `target/libs/`
   directory.

   ```shell
   ./mvnw --projects app dependency:tree
   ```

   In the output, focus on the section for `app`. You should see that Maven
   reports these direct 'dependencies:'

   ```
   ...
   [INFO] demo:app:jar:1.0.0
   [INFO] +- demo:B:jar:1.0.0:compile
   [INFO] \- demo:A:jar:1.1.0:compile
   ...
   ```

   That is the key distinction in this example:

   - Maven mediation has chosen `A` version `1.1.0` for the application
   - the runtime classpath still contains both `A-1.0.0.jar` and `A-1.1.0.jar`

   So the build tool has resolved the dependency graph, but the runtime layout
   is still ambiguous.

4. Run the application using the wildcard classpath that includes everything
  from `target/libs/`.

  This demonstrates that the JVM does not consult Maven’s dependency tree at
  runtime. It simply loads classes from the classpath entries it receives.

   ```shell
   java --class-path 'target/libs/*' demo.Main
   ```

   Observed output with the wildcard classpath

   ```
   Hello
   LibB: ¡Hola Mundo! This version has a bug!
   LibA: ¡Hola Mundo! This version has a bug!
   ```

   In this environment, the wildcard classpath results in the older `A`
   implementation being used. Notice that both `LibB` and the application’s
   direct call to `LibA` print the buggy message.

   That happens because both versions define the same class name, `demo_a.LibA`.
   Once the JVM has loaded that class from one JAR, every later reference to
   `demo_a.LibA` uses the already-loaded definition.

5. Run the same application again, but construct the classpath explicitly and put the newer
   `A` JAR first.

   The runtime behaviour changes without recompiling the application. The only thing that
   changed is classpath order.

   ```shell
   java \
     --class-path 'target/libs/A-1.1.0.jar:target/libs/B-1.0.0.jar:target/libs/app-1.0.0.jar' \
     demo.Main
   ```

   Observed output with the explicit classpath

   ```
   Hello
   LibB: Hello, World! Bug free, as you can see.
   LibA: Hello, World! Bug free, as you can see.
   ```

   Now both call sites use the fixed implementation from `A-1.1.0.jar`.

   This proves the real lesson of the example: when duplicate classes exist on
   the runtime classpath, the JVM uses whichever one it encounters first. That
   may or may not be the version your build tool intended.

   In this example, we loaded both JAR files, but that’s usually discouraged.
   Don’t load multiple versions of the same libaries in the classpath as this
   may have unexpected behaviour as shown here.

## Key takeaways and residual risk

- Maven dependency mediation and JVM class loading solve different problems; a
  clean dependency tree does not guarantee a safe or deterministic runtime
  classpath.
- The wildcard run demonstrates that duplicate classes can select the older
  `A-1.0.0.jar` implementation, while the explicit classpath selects
  `A-1.1.0.jar` without recompilation.
- Dependency management, exclusions, and deliberate runtime packaging reduce
  this ambiguity; avoid treating `lib/*` as a deployment policy.
- These checks are evidence for this workshop layout, not production approval. A
  human must review the resolved and packaged dependencies and make the release
  decision.
